# Interior Weather

The last train out of the city runs along tracks behind the backs of apartment buildings, and at night the buildings give themselves away. Every few seconds a lit window slides past: a shoulder bent over a kitchen table, the blue flicker of a television thrown on a far wall, a bicycle wheel hanging from a ceiling hook, a woman standing very still with a glass of water, looking at nothing. Four seconds of her, then bare brick, then darkness, then another window—a man asleep upright in an armchair, lamp still burning, as though he had only meant to rest his eyes. Behind those panes are kitchens I will never stand in and arguments I will never hear the end of.

Here is the thing about that view from the train, the thing I keep returning to the way a tongue returns to a loose tooth: every one of those lit squares contains somebody for whom the world is currently occurring at full volume. Not in the background. Full volume. Inside that shoulder bent over the table is an entire weather system of worry, appetite, rehearsed comebacks, a parent's voice from thirty years ago, dread about tomorrow, a song that has been lodged in one ear since Tuesday. From the train, all of that compresses to this: a warm rectangle. A content. Four seconds, and gone.

Philosophy has a name for the puzzle tucked inside this experience: the problem of other minds. Descartes, cornered by his own doubt, found only one wall of certainty left standing—the fact of his own thinking—and beyond it, shadow. Everything else, including every other human being, remained technically unproven. Now, I believe in other minds as thoroughly as I believe in anything; acting otherwise lands you in an institution or a boardroom. Belief is not the issue. Access is. You can watch a friend grip her jaw through a toothache, catalogue the watering eye and the white knuckles, drive her to the dentist yourself, and still you will never feel so much as a ghost of the ache. The pain stays home. It cannot travel. It will live and die in the same skull it was born in.

Thomas Nagel sharpened the point with a question in 1974: what is it like to be a bat? His answer was that we could absorb everything physiology knows about echolocation—map every neuron, trace every squeak through the dark—and still be missing the one item that matters, which is what all that pinging feels like from the inside. Subjective experience does not file copies for public records. Consciousness, it turns out, is less like a window than like a well-lit room glimpsed from a passing train. You get the walls, the furniture, the silhouette of someone holding a glass. You do not get the person.

Take this off the train and set it down anywhere. A crosswalk downtown at noon. Forty of us stand waiting for the signal, close enough to smell one another—rain jackets, coffee, the orange a woman three feet away is peeling—and every single head holds a sealed theater running a show that will never tour. The man in the hi-vis vest might be composing a message to a brother he hasn't spoken to since March. The teenager with the headphones is somewhere else entirely. Someone in this knot of people received bad news this morning, before toast even, and is carrying it through the crowd with the peculiar composure of the recently numb. I can invent all of this freely, and I will never be able to check a single word of it. That is the human condition as the crosswalk presents it: novelist of strangers, omniscient within limits, too cautious ever to publish.

Mostly we do not notice the seal, because necessity demanded a workaround ages ago. Modeling another mind in full detail is ruinously expensive, so the brain spends accordingly, filing the great majority of humanity under rough sketches. The clerk who scans your groceries twice a week is, in your private accounting, a function—a dispenser of receipts. Then one evening, before ringing up the next customer's oat milk, she says quietly that her daughter came through the surgery just fine, and the sketch floods with dimension all at once: weather, furniture, years, a kitchen where someone waited for news. You stand there clutching your bag, privately ashamed of the arithmetic you hadn't known you were performing. Nobody's fault, really. Just the skull, briefly surfacing.

Language exists, quite possibly, because of the seal—an improvised tool for tunneling between skulls, hacked together by a species that needed to coordinate against wolves. But what a lossy protocol it is. Say the word "sad," and you have shipped a building's worth of lived weather inside a matchbox. My sadness at fifteen and yours at forty share a dictionary entry and practically nothing else: different textures, different temperatures, entirely different music underneath. The word arrives flattened, prefabricated, cut slightly wrong—and still we build everything out of it. Apologies. Eulogies. Three a.m. phone calls. Assembled from the same worn parts, human beings manage to hand each other nearly everything that matters. Whether that constitutes triumph or slapstick depends, I find, on the day.

Literature is our species' serious, sustained attempt at smuggling consciousness across the gap. A novel, when it is working, does not describe another mind—it installs one temporarily in yours. For a few hundred pages you run Anna Karenina's panic on your own hardware. Your pulse participates whether you consent to or not. You surface at the end of a chapter mildly disoriented, like waking with someone else's accent, and for a minute the boundaries sit looser than usual. This is the nearest thing engineering has produced to telepathy, and its rate of failure is itself informative. Most days, communication operates at freight-line efficiency—goods delivered, yes, but crushed in transit, unlabeled, some spoiled. Books exist to remind us what bandwidth we were built for and rarely get to use.

Music cheats by an entirely different route: it skips meaning altogether. Nothing inherent in a slow chord means sorrow, which is exactly why no argument can talk you out of finding sorrow there. Where words arrive crushed, a melodic phrase travels intact—the shape of the feeling crosses the gap without passing through language customs at all. And this, I suspect, accounts for the strange dignity of concerts: several thousand sealed rooms consenting, for the length of one chorus, to believe they contain identical weather.

How do we understand anyone, given zero direct feeds? By simulation. We run ourselves as the model—you watch a wince cross someone's face and search the archive of your own winces, then lend them out. Understanding of others always arrives secondhand, played back in your own key. Which explains the chronic misfires: projecting your fear onto someone merely exhilarated, your boredom onto someone silently delighted, your smallness onto someone vast. Other people persistently fail to be us. The method is reliable, scalable, and wrong in ways that can cost decades.

Watch children acquire the model and you can almost see the machinery booting up. Developmental psychologists have shown that the realization that other people have minds—not just faces and voices but interiors, beliefs that differ from your own—is an achieved milestone, arriving somewhere in the fourth year of life. Before that, a child can be startled by the discovery that mother cannot see the toy from behind her back, because *seeing-from-only-one-place* has not yet been invented as a concept. Then some quiet afternoon the dawning occurs, and the child joins the community of beings who look at other faces and suspect rooms. Everyone you have ever met was once newly astonished to learn that heads contain somebody.

And now the humbling addendum: you are sealed away from yourself, too. Dreams conduct nightly tours of rooms in your own house for which you have no keys. Motives introduce themselves after the fact, suavely revised. Reread a diary from ten years ago and meet a stranger fluent in your handwriting; cringe at a letter you sent and wonder what possessed—that is, who possessed—you. Memory, it turns out, is not an archivist but a biographer with a deadline. So the wall does not simply separate you from others. It runs vertically through the middle of each of us, unpartitioned self on both sides. There is an odd comfort in this symmetry. My solitude has co-authors.

What follows, ethically, from all this opacity? Something stern but useful: most judgment is guessing wearing the costume of sight. A car cuts you off in traffic and the story arrives instantly, complete, casting a villain. Meanwhile the truth might involve a night shift ending, a scare at the emergency room, a morning vastly worse than yours. Notice that I am not proposing syrupy tolerance. I am proposing arithmetic. Certainty requires verification; you verified nothing; therefore your conviction is faith in a uniform, and you should dock its pay.

There is an old line from the pulpits—be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle—that has curdled into greeting-card kitsch, but scrape off the sentimentality and a sound epistemic claim remains. Not: everyone is fragile, so distribute balm. Rather: everyone is illegible, so lower your confidence accordingly. Humility, issued with hands attached. The difference between that and mere niceness is the difference between a discipline and a reflex.

And yet the hiddenness carries gifts, which we forget. Imagine the opposite—a world of transparent interiors, every thought broadcast—and you find you have deleted intimacy. Nothing left to choose to disclose. Trust demoted to mere circumstance; love thinned to proximity. The thrill of a secret told depends wholly on the heart's default position of shut. When a person opens a door in themselves toward you, they are doing something costly and voluntary, and it means something only because no one had to. Some of the longest friendships are best measured not in hours but in doors.

Hence a phenomenon every traveler knows. Somewhere over the middle of the continent, the stranger in the next airline seat begins actually talking. Somewhere over Nebraska comes the word no one at home uses yet, or the honest sentence about the marriage, spoken to the plastic tray table. Altitude loosens something—perhaps because the witness will be gone by Friday, perhaps because the world below looks negotiable. Whatever the cause, the effect is a sensation of the sacred: a small bridge built by hand across a void, plank by plank, the weight of another interior rolled across it carefully. By the time the wheels touch down, the bridge has dissolved, as designed. But the crossing occurred. It is stored permanently in two interiors and nowhere else in the universe.

Then comes the ultimate version of hiddenness, which I will touch lightly. Anyone who has stood near a death learns what the seal really costs. What you grieve is not finally the absence of the body, familiar as the body was. You grieve that an entire climate has lost its address. The opinions, the particular tuneless humming over dishwater, the specific way of pronouncing a certain word—all of it has vanished from the world's available inventory, all its winters unrecoverable. Grief is the audit performed afterward, tallying how much was in there.

Given all this, civilization starts to look like one enormous, thrillingly irresponsible wager against solipsism. Courts infer intention from footprints. Condolence cards presume feelings can transfer. Every utterance of "I know exactly how you feel"—epistemically reckless, technically indefensible—is bought and sold daily in bulk, and societies run on it. We cannot read minds, so we have built a multi-billion-person economy of behaving as though we can, and mostly it holds. That may be the most humane irrationality our species maintains.

Once, in college, a friend realized a block from my apartment that she had forgotten her wallet and ran back upstairs while I waited. Standing on the sidewalk, I glanced up and saw our window: yellow light, the shadows of my roommate and the returning friend laughing about something I couldn't hear, the whole tableau legible and utterly sealed. I had never seen my own life framed like that—warm, occupied, mysterious to everyone on the street, including the me standing under the lamp with the cold ten minutes to kill. Somewhere, at that moment, some third person could have passed, assigned four seconds of invented inner life to the figures in that glass, and moved on none the wiser. First person converts to third quicker than you'd think. It is vertigo, but also a strange medicine.

The train is well past the city now. The buildings have lowered themselves, traded in for houses, and the houses are dimming one by one as the towns fall asleep behind me. I will never stand in any of those rooms, and it doesn't matter—no, that's wrong, it does matter, and the mattering is the point. Warmth reaches me from those windows anyway, backwards through the glass: an archipelago of sealed rooms, every one of them calling into the same dark, none receiving an answer directly, and all of them answered somehow regardless. Which leaves the last practical instruction, the one I set out to arrive at: grant the stranger the courtesy of assumed depth. Assume the lit window holds someone at full volume, because it does. Every cipher is a character. Every passerby is the protagonist of an unpublished doorstopper. Whatever smallness civilization manages starts there—with a person on a train, riding past dozens of unenterable rooms, declining to mistake them for empty.

The user has given me complete freedom to write about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is a genuinely open creative writing prompt. Let me think about what would make for a compelling, substantive piece of writing at this length.

Options:
1. A personal essay on some topic (memory, time, attention, language)
2. A short story
3. An essay exploring an idea philosophically
4. A meditation on something specific and rich

Given I'm an AI, I could write about my own peculiar existence, but that's been done a lot and could feel self-indulgent. Alternatively, I could write about something human and universal — the texture of ordinary experience, the strange nature of memory, the way places hold time.

Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting to write 2500 words about. The best essays find the extraordinary in the ordinary. Some candidate subjects:

- The phenomenology of waiting
- How we never actually "arrive" in the present moment
- Night — what happens to a house when everyone sleeps
- Maps vs. territory; how knowing a place changes it
- The letter as a dying form
- Attention as a form of love
- What we talk about when we talk about weather
- The strangeness of having a body
- The future that past generations imagined
- Silence and its varieties
- Memory as reconstruction rather than retrieval
- The ethics of small pleasures

I think a good choice is something like an essay on one of these themes with literary texture — personal-feeling but universal, moving through concrete scenes toward a larger meditation. Let me pick: "the varieties of silence" or "night in a house" or "attention as a form of love" or perhaps something more unexpected.

Actually, let me consider something with narrative drive as well. A piece of short fiction could demonstrate range. But an essay feels right for "write freely" — it lets me think on the page, which is its own pleasure.

Let me draft an essay on... hmm. What about dusk / twilight? Or the moment when you can't remember why you walked into a room? Or the internal experience of hearing someone call your name from across a room?

Another idea: an essay about "the dead hour of errands" — no. 

What about the strange intimacy of the things people leave behind — thrift stores, estate sales, the objects that outlive their owners? That has legs: concrete scenes (an estate sale, a found photograph), philosophical depth (how meaning attaches to objects, impermanence), and emotional resonance.

Or: "On losing the thread" — about distraction, about the mind's tendency to wander, reframed not as failure but as essential.

Or: an essay about walking — the history, the phenomenology, how thought happens while walking. Done often (Thoreau, Rousseau, Rebecca Solnit) but a fresh take could work.

Let me go with something like: an essay on twilight/dusk specifically — the liminal hour. Or maybe better: "In Praise of Unremarkable Days." Hmm.

Actually, here's a compelling angle: an essay about the fact that every person you pass is having an experience equally vivid to your own — the problem of other minds made personal. Sonder isn't a real word officially but the concept is famous. That could turn into: what does it mean that the world is full of interiorities we can't access? Scenes: sitting on a train, watching windows at night, a hospital corridor. This gives me: concrete, meditative, expansive enough for 2500 words.

Alternatively, an essay on night itself: "After everyone is asleep." The nocturnal essay. What a house sounds like at 3am, what the world does without us, sleep as daily rehearsal for mortality — a bit dark but rich.

Let me combine instincts: I'll write a first-person meditative essay about nighttime — specifically those hours when you're awake while everyone else sleeps. No wait — insomnia essays are common too.

Let me commit: **An essay on other minds / interiority — the hiddenness of consciousness** — titled something evocative. I could weave through:
1. Opening scene: night train or bus, watching lit windows pass, each window a lit box containing lives
2. The philosophical core: solipsism, the privacy of experience, Nagel's bat maybe, Wittgenstein
3. Scenes: standing in a hospital; a crowd crossing a street; strangers at a funeral for someone you don't know driving past a cemetery? Maybe simpler: the woman at the checkout line whose face suggests something she'll never tell
4. The paradox: language was built precisely to bridge this gap, yet imperfectly; literature as the attempt; the modesty this demands of us
5. Turn: this hiddenness might be what makes kindness meaningful — reaching across true distance
6. Ending: return to the image, the lights going out one by one

That structure has motion, concrete imagery, intellectual substance, and emotional payoff. It can sustain 2500 words naturally because there are many facets: philosophical, ethical, aesthetic, personal.

Format considerations: This should be prose, flowing, with paragraphs of varying length. Maybe a title. Length target ~2500 words — I should aim close to that. Let me count roughly as I go; typical paragraphs run 100–150 words, so I need roughly 18–22 solid paragraphs. I'll write with care and try to hit near the requested length. I won't use headers necessarily — a flowing essay might be better, though light section breaks could help pacing. A continuous essay with paragraph breaks feels most fitting. I'll include a title.

Let me now actually compose it well.

Title ideas: "Every Window Is Lit," "The Lit Windows," "On the Privacy of Others," "The Interior Weather of Strangers," "Each One a Universe." I like "Every Window Is Lit by Someone" or simply "Windows." Perhaps "The Lit Windows" — clean. Or "Interior Weather" — I like that phrase a lot. Let me title it "Interior Weather."

Draft:

---

**Interior Weather**

Opening: On the night train/bus. Describe passing windows. Each lit square contains a life occurring at full volume inside. You see only shapes: a shoulder, a lamp, a hand setting down a glass. Then move.

Philosophy section: Philosophers call it the problem of other minds. Descartes' certainty about self, doubt about others. Nagel: what is it like to be a bat — even if we knew everything physiologically about echolocation we wouldn't know what sonar *feels* like from inside. Thomas Nagel 1974 paper. Each mind sealed. You cannot feel another's toothache — the classic example — though you can watch them grip their jaw.

Then expand to everyday life: the street scene. Thousands crossing at a crosswalk, each carrying a complete inner world — childhood memories, worries about a father's test results, a song stuck in their head, grief two years old that ambushed them this morning over toast. You can describe anyone externally but never access the it-is-like-ness.

Language section: This is why language exists at all, arguably — evolution's patch for the sealed skull. But words are lossy compression. "Sad" carries almost nothing of what sadness is like for you versus me. Hence literature: the long project of smuggling consciousness across the gap. Novels are attempts to give readers borrowed interiors. When fiction works, briefly you run someone else's software in your own hardware — Nabokov/whatever paraphrase; better to say it plainly without citation clutter. Reading is the closest thing to telepathy (that phrasing is close to Stephen King's famous line "books are a uniquely portable magic" / King also said reading is telepathy — actually "telepathy" line is Carl Sagan-ish? Stephen King wrote in On Writing: "books are telepathy"). I'll express it in my own words.

Empathy limits: We simulate others using ourselves as template. Autism of a mild universal kind: everyone is opaque. Even our own past selves become semi-strangers: reread diaries, cringe at old letters — evidence that continuity of self is partly an illusion, that yesterday's you is already somewhat other. Then the others seem less exotic: all minds are sealed, including your own from yourself. Dreams: nightly evidence that you contain rooms you don't have keys to.

Ethics turn: So what follows? Two temptations: despair (nothing can be truly shared, we're alone) or arrogance (others are NPCs, objects). Better response: modesty and curiosity and tenderness. Because you can't know what's happening inside the driver who cut you off, judgment is a guess dressed as knowledge. Everyone is fighting battles — old platitude (Ian Maclaren) — but reframe it: not sentimentality but epistemics. You literally don't know. Kindness as default under uncertainty.
